narrative:
The model predicted a 67.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your LSAT score, your class ranking in the third year of law school, and your undergraduate GPA. Your LSAT score of 23.5 was the strongest reason for the negative outcome; it is substantially below the average of 37 seen among accepted students and strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your third-year class ranking in the second decile was the second most important factor. This ranking is also much lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted applicants, further increasing the model’s estimate of failure risk. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 worked in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted chance of failure, but its positive effect was not large enough to offset the other two factors.

Although your family income, gender, race, and full-time status were considered, none of them played a meaningful role in the final decision.

To improve your chances in a future application, focus on raising your LSAT score and strengthening your academic performance so that both your test results and class standing move closer to the levels typical of admitted students. Retaking the LSAT after targeted preparation is likely the highest-impact step you can take next.
